catalog_quote: One cannot talk about Tùtrùgbù without referring to tones. Like many West African languages, Tùtrùgbù is a tone language because it combines consonants, vowels and tone to form morphemes. ... Tùtrùgbù, as already mentioned, is a tone language with three level tones namely High, Mid, and Low in addition to two contour tones which are Rising and Falling. ... Lexically, tones are used to show difference in meaning in words in the language. ... When it bears the high tone, it means grow as in shɛ́ „grow‟ and when it bears a low tone, it means past tense of the verb go as in shɛ̀ „left‟. ... [loanwords, 4.2.3.1:] The tone combinations reported from Buli is observed in Tùtrùgbù. ... a) ˈbᴧkɩt → bókítì „bucket‟ b) ˈsəʊʤə → sódzà „soldier‟ c) ˈmætʃɩz → mádzésì „matches‟ ... In the examples above, all the loanwords with primary stress in the source language were assigned high tone in the target …

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Gborsi 2015 text we hold at the stated sections/pages (3.4.0 pp. 65-66; 3.4.2 pp. 68-69; 3.4.3.1 p. 72; 4.2.3.1 pp. 118-119). The thesis is a dedicated 182-pp phonology with a tone chapter; 'stress' appears only in English-loanword tone assignment, so the 'tonal, no word-stress rule described' coding is faithful. Web/Glottolog check: the descriptive literature is small (7 Glottolog items). The one open phonology article (McCollum & Essegbey 2020, PDA, CC BY) was downloaded and read: it treats Tutrugbu as tonal (H/M/L + contours, possible super-high), uses 'initial prominence' strictly as edge privilege for vowel harmony, and says metrical prominence is not relevant (p. 11) - confirms the classification. sources.quote: No word stress is posited; 'prominence' in the title is initial-syllable edge prominence used to derive progressive labial harmony on prefixes. Tone: three level tones (H, M, L), a potential fourth super-high level in some data, falling and rising contours. Metrical (stress) prominence explicitly declared not relevant to Tutrugbu.
sources.locator: fn. 4, p. 4 (tone marking: acute = H, macron = M, low unmarked; possible fourth super-high level; circumflex falling, caron rising); p. 11 ('Since metrical prominence is not relevant for the analysis of Tutrugbu we do not discuss it.. and instead center our attention on edge prominence')
sources.note: Only other Glottolog phonology item; title says 'initial prominence', which needed checking against a tonal/no-stress coding. downloaded: prominence is edge privilege for harmony, metrical prominence declared not relevant (p. 11); tone footnote (p. 4) matches Gborsi.

Reading sec. 2.4 would confirm that no word stress is posited and settle the number of level tones (PDA 2020 fn. 4 mentions a possible fourth, super-high).
